question.text: Under Section 45 of the Insurance Act, a life insurance policy becomes incontestable after a specified period from the date of policy commencement, risk commencement, or revival, whichever is later. What is this period?

explanation.text: The Logic: Section 45 of the Insurance Act provides that a life insurance policy cannot be called into question after 3 years from the date of issuance of the policy, the date of commencement of risk, the date of revival of the policy, or the date of any rider, whichever is later. Once this 3-year period has elapsed, the workbook states that a death claim under a life insurance policy cannot be denied on any ground. The Trap: 5 years is the moratorium period applicable to health insurance, not life insurance, and is a common point of confusion with the 3-year life-insurance contestability period. 2 years was the older provision before Section 45 was amended. 7 years has no statutory basis here. Note: During the first 3 years, an insurer may contest a life insurance claim on grounds such as fraud or misrepresentation; once the 3-year period under Section 45 is over, the policy/death claim cannot be questioned on any ground per the workbook.
